Implement the following change in this repository. Do not install dependencies or run the full test suite; run the tests relevant to your change if you want to. Make the code change (and adjust or add a test if it is natural), then summarize what you changed and why. A Python environment with this project installed is at bench-venv: run a test file with `PYTHONPATH=. /Users/yoavshmariahu/src/thinker/bench/repos/mlflow-venv/bin/python -m pytest <path>`.

Custom scorers written with the scorer decorator carry their function source code, and loading one runs that code. Today this happens inside the tracking server itself, for example when a scorer is invoked, when online-scoring settings are validated, and when gateway guardrails are loaded. That means user-supplied code can run in the server process, which is a security problem. Desired behavior: the server must never execute custom scorer code. In the server, a custom scorer should load as inert metadata that keeps its fields and serialized form, so it can be inspected and passed along to the job executor, but running it must raise an error. The job executor should still rebuild and run custom scorers as before, and a regular client process, such as a user loading a registered scorer to run locally, should behave exactly as it does now. This refusal must be enforced at the point where scorers are rebuilt, so a future code path in the server can't bypass it, and the server must not be able to pick up executor permission from its surrounding environment. Gateway guardrails run inside the server, so custom decorator-based scorers must be rejected as guardrails, both when a guardrail is created and when one is loaded. This includes ensembles that contain a custom scorer. Built-in scorers and judges created with the judge-making helper must keep working. If an endpoint already has a guardrail backed by a custom scorer, requests to it should fail with a server error that names the guardrail, instead of silently skipping it and serving traffic unprotected. Other guardrail loading failures should still be skipped and logged as they are now. A custom scorer refused as a guardrail raises `UnsupportedGuardrailScorerError`, defined in `mlflow.gateway.guardrails`.
tasks.goldTitle: Confine custom scorer code execution to the job executor

acceptance.criterion: When a custom scorer defined with the scorer decorator is loaded/rebuilt from its serialized form inside the tracking server process (e.g. during online-scoring validation or gateway guardrail loading), the resulting object still exposes the scorer's normal fields (name, description, aggregations, source) and still serializes back to the same data, but invoking/running it in that process raises an error instead of executing the stored function body.
A custom scorer submitted to run via the job executor (job execution enabled) is still rebuilt and actually executed, producing a real scoring result, exactly as before this change.

A regular client process (not the tracking server) that loads a registered custom scorer and runs it locally behaves exactly as it did before this change (same success/failure conditions, e.g. still gated by the existing Databricks/local-opt-in rules), with no new restriction introduced for that case.

Creating a gateway guardrail from a custom (scorer-decorator) scorer, or loading/resolving an already-created guardrail that is backed by a custom scorer -- including an ensemble that contains a custom scorer among its sub-scorers -- raises `UnsupportedGuardrailScorerError` (importable from `mlflow.gateway.guardrails`) instead of running the scorer's code.

Guardrails backed by built-in scorers or by judges created with the judge-making helper (make_judge) still create and load successfully and run correctly, unaffected by the new restriction on custom scorers.

At request time, a gateway endpoint whose configuration includes a guardrail backed by a custom scorer responds with a server-side error that names the failing guardrail (not a silently-skipped guardrail serving unprotected traffic), while any other, unrelated guardrail-loading failure for that same endpoint is still skipped and logged rather than failing the request.

When the AI Gateway streams a response containing multiple parallel tool calls through the Gemini or LiteLLM providers, every tool call is reported with the same position (index 0). Clients that assemble streamed tool calls by index then merge separate calls into one, concatenating their arguments into a single broken call. For Gemini, each tool call arrives whole, so two calls in the same streamed chunk both show index 0, and calls arriving in later chunks also restart at 0. For LiteLLM, the index that the underlying library supplies on each chunk is ignored and replaced with the call's position within that chunk, so interleaved chunks for call 0 and call 1 all end up as 0. Desired behavior: for Gemini, tool calls should get consecutive indices across the whole stream, so calls in one chunk are numbered 0, 1, and so on, and calls in later chunks continue the numbering. For LiteLLM, the index provided on each streamed chunk should be preserved, falling back to the call's position in the chunk only when none is provided. That way, arguments for each call are merged correctly per index. Two issues are out of scope: Gemini's finish reason never reporting tool calls, and the Bedrock index offset after a text block.

Details the tests check:
For Gemini, number tool calls separately for each candidate (each streamed choice): within one candidate, its tool calls get 0, 1, 2, and so on across the whole stream. Each streamed chunk's choice index is the candidate's own `index` field from the Gemini response when it has one, and its position in the candidates list otherwise.

Implement the following change in this repository. Do not install dependencies or run the full test suite; run the tests relevant to your change if you want to. Make the code change (and adjust or add a test if it is natural), then summarize what you changed and why. A Python environment with this project installed is at bench-venv: run a test file with `PYTHONPATH=. /Users/yoavshmariahu/src/thinker/bench/repos/mlflow-venv/bin/python -m pytest <path>`.

When the tracking server is under heavy load and its shared pool of worker threads for handling requests is fully occupied, the server-info endpoint (the one clients use to discover server capabilities) stops responding. It hangs or times out along with every other request, even though it only returns a small, static piece of information. This makes capability discovery unreliable exactly when the server is busiest. The endpoint should keep responding promptly even when the shared worker pool is exhausted, by being handled with its own dedicated, separate capacity. This applies to both the standard API path and the equivalent path used by the web UI's AJAX calls. The response content must stay exactly the same as before. The endpoint must remain publicly accessible without authentication, including when a custom static prefix is configured for the server. Deployments that run under other server setups (such as Gunicorn or Waitress) must continue to serve the same server-info response as they do today.

Details the tests check:
Serve the server-info endpoint from a new FastAPI router named `server_info_router`, importable from `mlflow.server.fastapi_app` beside the other native routers, with its response built by a new function `build_server_info_payload()` (no arguments) in a new module `mlflow.server.server_info_api`; tests replace that function to simulate errors. When it raises an `MlflowException`, respond with the exception's `get_http_status_code()` and its `serialize_as_json()` body, as the Flask handler does. The health check (`/health` and `/mlflow/health`, answering "OK") must also keep responding while the shared worker pool is exhausted, through the same dedicated capacity. With basic auth on, the server-info paths are public, as `/health` is: `mlflow.server.auth.is_unprotected_route(path)` returns true for them, with and without the static prefix.

+"""Shared HTTP responses for MLflow exceptions."""
+
+import logging
+
+from starlette.responses import Response
+
+from mlflow.exceptions import MlflowException
+
+_logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
+
+
+def mlflow_exception_response(exc: MlflowException, *, handler_name: str) -> Response:
+    """Return Flask's exact ``serialize_as_json()`` body."""
+    status_code = exc.get_http_status_code()
+    if status_code >= 500:
+        is_debug = _logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG)
+        msg = f"Error in {handler_name}: {exc}"
+        if not is_debug:
+            msg += ". Set MLFLOW_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG for traceback."
+        _logger.error(msg, exc_info=is_debug)
+    return Response(
+        content=exc.serialize_as_json(),
+        media_type="application/json",
+        status_code=status_code,
+    )

When I stream a response through the AI Gateway's Anthropic provider and the model makes parallel tool calls, the calls get merged into one. Every tool call is reported with index 0, the second call is placed in the second choice instead of the first, and the finish event is sent once per content block instead of once at the end. Clients that read only the first choice and merge tool-call fragments by index (such as the OpenAI Python client and LangChain) end up with a single tool call whose arguments are the concatenation of both calls' arguments. The same problem can occur when a text block comes before a tool call, because the tool call's position then depends on the text block's position. Streaming should number tool calls sequentially from 0 in the order they appear, regardless of any text blocks before them. Every streamed chunk should use only the first choice. The finish event should be emitted exactly once per response. Non-streaming behavior should stay as it is.
tasks.goldTitle: Fix parallel tool call indices in Anthropic streaming

acceptance.criterion: Streaming a response containing two (or more) parallel tool calls numbers the tool-call deltas sequentially starting at 0 in the order the calls appear (first call's delta chunks use index 0, second call's chunks use index 1, etc.), rather than every chunk reporting index 0.

When a text content block precedes a parallel tool call in the model's output, the tool call's delta index still starts counting from 0 among tool calls and is unaffected by the position/index of the preceding text block.

Every chunk emitted while streaming a chat completion contains exactly one choice (the first choice), regardless of how many content blocks (text and/or tool calls) the underlying model streamed, so a second tool call is never placed into a second choice.
For a given streamed chat completion response, a finish event (a chunk with a non-null finish_reason) is emitted exactly once, at the end of the stream, rather than once per content block.
Non-streaming chat completion responses (including ones with one or more tool calls) are unaffected by this change and keep returning a single choice with the tool calls as before.

When validating a candidate model against a baseline, the minimum relative change threshold gives wrong results if the baseline metric value is negative. For example, with a baseline R² of -1.8 and a 5% required improvement, a clearly worse candidate at -5.0 passes validation, while a perfect candidate at 1.0 fails. The relative change is currently computed by dividing the difference by the signed baseline value, which flips the direction of the comparison for negative baselines. The relative change should instead be measured against the magnitude (absolute value) of the baseline, for both metrics where higher is better and metrics where lower is better. Behavior for positive baselines must stay exactly the same, and the existing zero-baseline handling (falling back to a plain comparison) must not change. The documentation describing the threshold should also be corrected to state the required value as the baseline plus the relative change times the baseline's magnitude (and the lower-is-better counterpart), noting that this matches the old formula when the baseline is positive.

Converting a dataset into an evaluation dataset fails with an error when the dataset contains nested arrays of varying lengths whose elements are dictionaries. For example, a Hugging Face dataset where each row holds a list of dictionaries, and the lists differ in length from row to row. The failure happens while the dataset's content is being hashed (fingerprinted). The hashing step tries to turn the irregular nested data into a uniform rectangular array, and that is impossible when lengths differ, so a value error is raised and the conversion aborts. Datasets with uniform, regular shapes work fine. Converting such datasets should succeed instead of raising an error. When the data can't be made into a uniform array and contains dictionaries, hashing should fall back to a general approach that walks through the nested contents item by item. Hashing should still produce a consistent result, so the same data gives the same hash every time.

Details the tests check:
The same fallback also covers ragged nested arrays whose elements are not dictionaries (for example rows [[1, 2], [3]]): they hash without an error, and data that differs only in how elements are split across rows ([[1, 2], [3]] against [[1], [2, 3]]) hashes differently. Rows that are missing (None or NaN), at any position including the first row, are handled by it too: the array hashes without an error, and the same data always hashes the same.

When the irregular nested data contains dictionaries and cannot be converted into a uniform rectangular array, hashing falls back to walking through the nested contents item by item rather than failing, and this fallback path is actually exercised (not just caught and silently ignored) for such inputs.
Hashing the same irregular (varying-length, dict-containing) data twice yields an identical hash each time, i.e. the fallback hashing is deterministic.
Datasets with uniform/regular shapes (including existing list-of-dict and nested-array cases) continue to hash successfully and existing hashing/digest tests for evaluation datasets still pass.

Converting a dataset with mismatched row lengths that do not contain dictionaries (plain irregular numeric/scalar data) still raises the existing validation error rather than being silently absorbed by the new dict-specific fallback.

tasks.goldTitle: Honor `tool_choice` in Gemini and Vertex AI gateway requests

acceptance.criterion: A chat request (non-streaming) to a Gemini or Vertex AI gateway endpoint that declares tools and sets tool_choice to "required" results in the outbound request to the provider carrying a tool-calling configuration that forces a function call (Gemini's ANY mode), rather than leaving tool selection to the model's default automatic behavior.

A chat request that declares tools and sets tool_choice to "none" results in the outbound request carrying a tool-calling configuration that disables function calling (Gemini's NONE mode), so the provider is instructed not to call any tool.

A chat request that declares multiple tools and sets tool_choice to a specific named function results in the outbound request restricting tool calling to only that named function, even though other tools were declared.
This tool_choice handling applies identically to streaming chat requests, not just non-streaming ones.

When tool_choice is omitted or set to "auto", the outbound request is unchanged from current behavior (no forced/none/restricted tool-calling configuration is added), and when no tools are declared in the request at all, no tool-calling configuration is sent regardless of any tool_choice value.
Existing Gemini/Vertex AI gateway provider tests still pass.
